title: Ezekiel 44:15–31
context: The LORD continues. The Levitical priests, the sons of Zadok, who kept charge of the sanctuary when Israel went astray, will come near to minister and offer the fat and the blood. Zadok served as priest under David and Solomon (1 Kings 1:39; 2:35), and Ezekiel consistently reserves the altar for his line (40:46; 43:19; 48:11); how this relates to earlier priestly history is discussed by interpreters, and the text presents it as a reward for faithfulness. The priests are to wear linen in the inner court and change before going to the people; not shave their heads or let their hair grow long; drink no wine in the inner court; marry within set limits; teach the difference between holy and common and clean and unclean; judge disputes by the LORD’s ordinances; keep the feasts and Sabbaths; avoid defilement from the dead except for close family; and offer a sin offering when returning to service. The LORD himself is their inheritance, and they receive the offerings, first fruits, and devoted things. Many of these rules echo the law of Moses (compare Leviticus 10:9–10; 21:1–7; Numbers 18:12–20), though some details differ, such as the marriage rule in 44:22 compared with Leviticus 21:7 and 21:14; these are best read as given, without forcing them to match. The mention of sacrifices raises a question readers handle differently. Some who expect a literal future temple see memorial or purifying offerings, while others read the sacrifices as Ezekiel’s picture of restored worship in the terms of his day, fulfilled in Christ’s “one sacrifice for sins forever” (Hebrews 10:12; compare 10:18). Both views are held among Arminian and Reformed readers. Readers in both traditions take the temple vision of chapters 40–48 in the ways named at 40:1–16. Arminian and Reformed readers generally treat the call to holy service and the LORD as the priests’ portion as shared ground.

verses.text: “ ‘ “But the Levitical priests, the sons of Zadok, who performed the duty of my sanctuary when the children of Israel went astray from me, shall come near to me to minister to me. They shall stand before me to offer to me the fat and the blood,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sons of Zadok, who stayed faithful when Israel went astray, coming near to minister and offer the fat and the blood. Faithfulness is honored.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God rewarding the faithful line of Zadok (compare 1 Kings 2:35; 1 Samuel 2:35). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse in its historical setting, held with care.

verses.text: “They shall enter into my sanctuary, and they shall come near to my table, to minister to me, and they shall keep my instruction.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Zadokite priests entering the sanctuary, approaching the table, and keeping God’s instruction. Nearness to God comes with responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the privilege of drawing near to minister before God. Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about faithful service in God’s presence.

verses.text: “ ‘ “It will be that when they enter in at the gates of the inner court, they shall be clothed with linen garments. No wool shall come on them while they minister in the gates of the inner court, and within.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the priests wearing linen, not wool, in the inner court. Their clothing marks the holiness of their service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an echo of the linen garments of the law (compare Exodus 28:39; Leviticus 16:4). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the vision’s ordered worship.

verses.text: They shall have linen turbans on their heads, and shall have linen trousers on their waists. They shall not clothe themselves with anything that makes them sweat.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see linen turbans and trousers, and nothing that makes the priests sweat. Service before God is to be clean and orderly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see attention to purity and dignity in worship (compare Exodus 28:42). Both traditions commonly read the verse in its temple setting without pressing every detail.

verses.text: When they go out into the outer court, even into the outer court to the people, they shall put off their garments in which they minister and lay them in the holy rooms. They shall put on other garments, that they not sanctify the people with their garments.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the priests changing garments before going out to the people. Holy things are kept separate from common use.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the distinction between holy and common carefully guarded (compare Leviticus 16:23). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the vision’s holiness rules.

verses.text: “ ‘ “They shall not shave their heads, or allow their locks to grow long. They shall only cut off the hair of their heads.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the priests neither shaving their heads nor letting their hair grow long, but trimming it. Moderation marks their appearance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an echo of priestly rules in Leviticus 21:5. Both traditions commonly read the verse as describing ordered conduct for those who serve.

verses.text: None of the priests shall drink wine when they enter into the inner court.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the priests forbidden to drink wine when entering the inner court. Clear minds are needed for holy service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same rule given in Leviticus 10:9. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about sober, attentive service.

verses.text: They shall not take for their wives a widow, or her who is put away; but they shall take virgins of the offspring of the house of Israel, or a widow who is the widow of a priest.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see marriage limits for the priests, who may marry virgins of Israel or a priest’s widow. Their households reflect their calling.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see rules that resemble but do not exactly match Leviticus 21:7 and 21:14. Both traditions commonly read the verse as given, without forcing the details to align.

verses.text: They shall teach my people the difference between the holy and the common, and cause them to discern between the unclean and the clean.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the priests teaching the difference between holy and common, clean and unclean. Teaching is central to their role.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the priests correcting the failure named in 22:26 (compare Leviticus 10:10; Malachi 2:7). Readers in both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground about teaching God’s ways.

verses.text: “ ‘ “In a controversy they shall stand to judge. They shall judge it according to my ordinances. They shall keep my laws and my statutes in all my appointed feasts. They shall make my Sabbaths holy.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the priests judging disputes by God’s ordinances and keeping his feasts and Sabbaths. Justice and worship belong together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the priests’ judicial role as in Deuteronomy 17:9. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that God’s law governs both worship and justice.

verses.text: “ ‘ “They shall go in to no dead person to defile themselves; but for father, or for mother, or for son, or for daughter, for brother, or for sister who has had no husband, they may defile themselves.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the priests avoiding defilement from the dead except for close family. Compassion for family is allowed within holiness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an echo of Leviticus 21:1–2. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as balancing holiness with natural grief.

verses.text: After he is cleansed, they shall reckon to him seven days.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see seven days counted after a priest’s cleansing. Purification takes time and is not rushed, even for those who serve at the altar.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the waiting period as a sign that defilement is taken seriously (compare Numbers 19:11). Both traditions commonly read the verse within the vision’s purity rules, without pressing beyond it.

verses.text: In the day that he goes into the sanctuary, into the inner court, to minister in the sanctuary, he shall offer his sin offering,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the priest offering a sin offering when he returns to minister. Readers hold several views of such offerings in light of Hebrews 10.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same offering and note the question raised by Hebrews 10:12, 18. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the main readings of these sacrifices with care, without declaring a winner.

verses.text: “ ‘They shall have an inheritance: I am their inheritance; and you shall give them no possession in Israel. I am their possession.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he is the priests’ inheritance and possession. Their portion is God himself, not land or wealth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the echo of Numbers 18:20 and Deuteronomy 18:2. Both traditions commonly hold this as shared ground about God as the portion of those who serve him (compare Psalm 73:26).

verses.text: They shall eat the meal offering, and the sin offering, and the trespass offering; and every devoted thing in Israel shall be theirs.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the priests eating the meal, sin, and trespass offerings and receiving devoted things. Their needs are met through worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see provision for the priests as in Numbers 18:14. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse in light of the sacrifice question, holding the main readings with care.

verses.text: The first of all the first fruits of every thing, and every offering of everything, of all your offerings, shall be for the priest. You shall also give to the priests the first of your dough, to cause a blessing to rest on your house.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the first fruits and offerings given to the priests, so that blessing rests on the people’s houses. Generosity brings blessing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an echo of Numbers 18:12. Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about honoring God with the first of what he gives.

verses.text: The priests shall not eat of anything that dies of itself or is torn, whether it is bird or animal.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the priests forbidden to eat anything that dies of itself or is torn. Purity extends to their food.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an echo of Leviticus 22:8. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the vision’s detailed picture of holy service.
